stories.headline: Barcelona's Anthony Gordon ahead of Aston Villa: 'I can do a lot more'
stories.summary: Anthony Gordon said Barcelona have not seen the best of him yet as he promises to become more selfish ahead of Tuesday's Champions League game vs. Aston Villa.
stories.body:
BARCELONA -- Anthony Gordon said Barcelona have not seen the best of him yet as he promises to become more selfish ahead of Tuesday's Champions League game against Aston Villa at Spotify Camp Nou.

Gordon, a €70 million summer signing from Newcastle United, has made an encouraging start to life at Barça, scoring three goals and providing five assists so far.

The England international's most recent goal came in Saturday's 6-1 victory over Alavés, a lovely dinked finish over the goalkeeper, but he says there is more to come as he prepares to face Premier League opposition for the first time since moving to Spain.

"I have started quite well considering it's a new country for me, maybe 7.5 out of 10," he said in a news conference on Monday.

"It's a massive change. It's a new team, although the new country is the biggest part. I have started well, but I can do a lot more.

"It will take some time for me to really settle and grow. When this happens, you will see the very best of me, which you definitely haven't seen so far."

To reach the next level, Gordon says he is aware he must be more selfish at times.

"My demands are always the same, to score, to assist, to be someone who can change a game in any moment and to take responsibility for the game," he said.

"The best in history do this, so that is what I chase. I think I can do it more, be more selfish sometimes, dribble and shoot more. This is the big focus -- definitely to score more goals.

"The challenge here at Barça is different to what I had before. At Everton, I was fighting relegation, which was tough; Newcastle's [objective] was [to quality for the] Champions League or to push up the table.

"Now it's trophies, so three very different challenges. I have really enjoyed all three. To be competing on every front, for every trophy, is definitely the most enjoyable.

"People think that is more pressure, but it's better pressure than fighting relegation or trying to climb the table."

During a recent international break, Gordon suggested he has gained a newfound respect back in his native England after moving to Barcelona in the summer.

However, he wanted to clarify that he did not mean people had a negative opinion of in his homeland, just that Barça's style of play gives him the chance to showcase other attributes.

"When I said that, I didn't mean people were judging me wrong," he said.

"I meant they had never seen me in a system that highlights these qualities. Like I said before, I have played in three different styles of team; that probably shows the intelligence I am talking about to be able to succeed in all three.

"I wasn't saying people judge me wrong or have a negative perspective of me, just that they hadn't seen me in this kind of system before, which I think now is helping them appreciate me a little bit more."

Barça's rout of Alavés at the weekend was a return to winning ways after back-to-back losses to Paris Saint-Germain and Real Madrid.

Those defeat have raised some doubts about Hansi Flick's team in big games ahead of a week which will see them face Villa and then Atlético Madrid, but Gordon believes the LaLiga leaders can compete with anyone.

"I don't think PSG or Madrid are above us," he insisted. "We have to take responsibility for both losses. They are the two biggest games this season so far and we lost.

"But they are not above us. We are fantastic and on our day can beat anyone."

Next up for Gordon is Unai Emery's Villa, who have won all three of their Champions League games this season, leaving them three points ahead of Barça in the standings heading into Tueday's meeting.

"They are a very good team," Gordon said. "I played against them a couple of times with mixed success.

"They have a great coach [Emery], one of the best in the world right now. They are on a great run as of late. It's a tough challenge, but I am very excited."

stories.headline: Arsenal got a big win at Liverpool, but why no Isak penalty?
stories.summary: Arsenal got a big win at Liverpool to go clear atop the Premier League, but Liverpool should have had a penalty. Plus: Michael Carrick's Man United future, Milan's bounce-back, Bayern's frustrations and more.
stories.body:
What a weekend in soccer! Europe's top leagues delivered, as they always do, when it comes to talking points.

In the Premier League's big games, Arsenal got a huge win (and a little luck) Sunday in breaking a historic winless streak at Liverpool dating back to 2012, while Man United sank from bad to worse in losing heavily at Chelsea on Saturday.

In LaLiga, Real Madrid got a win that should make Jose Mourinho happy for how they did it (scoring early and often), while Bayern Munich drew against Borussia Dortmund in Der Klassiker, a game they really, really should have won. In Serie A, Ruben Amorim (remember him, Man United fans?) and Milan won the derby over Inter to cap a tough week in the best possible way. We also got narratives galore from Brighton (how do they keep doing it?), Tottenham (yes, they're back), Juventus (shoutout to Kerim Alajbegovic), Barcelona (who rebounded from the Clasico loss in fine fashion) and much more.

It's Monday morning, so what better time for some musings? Let's get into it.

- United implode at Chelsea; they are now in Premier League relegation battle

- Arsenal hold on for a big win at Liverpool, one Iraola & Co. can learn from

- What soccer stars did for Halloween: James the Joker, DracuLucas, more

Arsenal get big win at Liverpool, but referees owe us answers

I'll get this out of the way and get to what we really want to talk about which is, you know, football.

Liverpool should have had a penalty for Jurriën Timber's shirt-pull on Alexander Isak -- there's really no gray area. If referee Andy Madley didn't see it clearly or deemed it (as some have suggested) "normal physical jockeying," VAR Stuart Attwell should have sent him to the monitor to have another look. There's nothing normal about grabbing an opponent's shirt, and it doesn't take a physicist to figure out that without the tug, Isak would have headed the ball goalward.

In fact, it could have been a denial of goal-scoring opportunity (DOGSO) situation. Law 12 is pretty clear: "Where a player ... denies an obvious goal-scoring opportunity and the referee awards a penalty kick, the offender is cautioned if the offence was an attempt to play the ball or a challenge for the ball: in all other circumstances [holding, pulling, pushing, etc.] the offending player must be sent off."

This is as open and shut as you're going to see. And please, don't spread the nonsense theory that Isak "should have made more of the pull" to influence the ref. I don't want to see players trying to "win" penalties, and certainly not when it's that obvious. I just want the VAR to help the referee do his job. (And I'm pretty sure Andoni Iraola feels the same way despite what he said postgame.)

Heck, later in the same game we had a perfect example of a player "making the most of it" to try to influence the referee. Alexis Mac Allister throwing himself to the ground, and staying there, writhing in pain, after being brushed by Noni Madueke's forehead was simply embarrassing. It's pretty much the very definition of "unsporting behavior," which is a cautionable offense. Mac Allister did get a yellow, but we don't know whether it was for that or for moments earlier, when he leaned over a prone Martin Odegaard and talked trash before tapping him on the head.

On to the football. The three points are big for Arsenal. Their 1-0 victory -- and first at Anfield in 14 years -- reinforces the notion that they're an elite defensive team that is willing to get physical and humble to defend the lead.

There are two elements to that. First, while it's true that those attributes are critical at times, I'd feel better about them if they kept creating chances after taking the lead. The goal -- starting with the clockwork press and continuing through Declan Rice's intelligent run -- was hugely impressive. But for the remaining 74 minutes, they managed just 0.30 xG.

Second, while the stat of holding Liverpool to zero shots on target at home for the first time since they started keeping track sounds impressive, the fact is they gave up 17 shots and spent longer than Mikel Arteta would have wanted in their own area. This team can kick it up several notches. While this may be enough to win the Premier League, if they want to take the next step in Europe, they'll probably have to. It's one thing to sit and defend against Isak and Bradley Barcola, another to do it against Lamine Yamal and Raphinha.

As for Liverpool, I know effort and belief are supposed to be taken for granted, but that part was still impressive. Missing was their quality, and you're not going to fix that overnight. Dominik Szoboszlai's return should help, but the elephant in the room remains the middle of the park. Playing a midfield two is tough enough with this front four; doing so with this crew is even harder. Throw in the fact that they're still learning on the fly under Iraola, and it's hard to see how this can be anything other than a rebuilding, transition season.

Emphatic derby win caps perfect bounce-back for Amorim, AC Milan

On Wednesday, they conceded three silly goals and lost at home to Bologna. On Thursday, they unveiled plans for a new 71,500-seat stadium and a naming rights agreement reportedly worth a whopping €650 million ($725 million U.S.) over 20 years -- the most lucrative around, U.S. stadiums included. And on Saturday, they defeated Internazionale 3-1 in the derby.

Yeah, you could say it was a pretty nifty turnaround for Milan in the space of 72 hours.

They're still fifth in the table, mind you -- a whopping seven points behind Lazio, the little engine that could. It's the fourth derby win in a row for the Rossoneri, so if they don't follow it up with real achievement in Serie A and the UEFA Europa League, it will feel pretty hollow. And if you really want to be a Debbie Downer, Inter won the xG battle, Adrien Rabiot's goal was probably a mishit (if it was meant to be a pass, well, there was nobody in that area, so it wasn't a good pass) and Mike Maignan had to pull off a miracle save on Djed Spence at 2-1.

But so what? Milan were entertaining -- none more so than Diego Moreira, who rampaged down the right flank and scored a sumptuous free kick. Luka Modric showed (once more) that if you manage his minutes, he can be a game changer, Christian Pulisic scored again and Yunus Musah monstered the Inter midfield. Not bad for a club that, in the space of five months, changed its coach, sporting director, center forward, wing backs and CEO.

It's also a personal victory for Amorim. He's less tethered to the orthodoxy of the 3-4-2-1 dogma of the past, more in sync with the players at his disposal (some of whom show marked improvement over past years) and unafraid to put his faith in youngsters.

At first glance, the big takeaway for Inter is that with Lautaro Martínez injured and the other two forwards (Ange-Yoan Bonny and Pio Esposito) struck down by the flu, they had no option but to play a lone striker. Those absences messed up Christian Chivu's entire approach, but that's a bit of a red herring. Sure, Inter would probably have been better with a full complement of strikers at their disposal, but they had plenty of the ball, plenty of touches in the opposition box and plenty of chances. What they missed was the execution from their one fit striker, Marcus Thuram, and the usually dependable duo of Nicolò Barella and Hakan Çalhanoglu, who were effectively shut down.

Chivu said after the game that they were lacking intensity. Maybe so, but it sounded like coach-speak. Maybe it was the fact that for the sixth time this season they went two goals down, which really shouldn't be happening to a side with this much talent. That speaks more to mindset and approach (they were 2-0 down after just 10 minutes) than the usual cliches. Maybe they felt that, having come from behind so many times before, they'd do so again. If that's the case, some humility wouldn't go amiss.

The good news is that Chivu is a calming influence and you imagine they'll treat this as a bump in the road, nothing more. If that doesn't happen, they're in trouble.

Defeat at Chelsea should make no difference to Michael Carrick's future

Yeah, I would have made the exact same point if Manchester United had converted some of those first-half chances that they squandered miserably and taken all three points, rather than collapsing in the second half and losing 2-0. Carrick is not the only problem at United -- far from it. But he's also not the solution, and because his bosses are unlikely to sack themselves and you can't dump anywhere near the number of players who should be dumped, guess who's going to be the scapegoat?

And you would imagine they'll do it not with any sort of vision in mind, but in search of the proverbial "shakeup" and "new manager bounce" -- all the stupid clichés that turn out to be true because many players are ultimately just overgrown teens.

This is Man United's worst start since the 1980s, and anyone who affects surprise after their third-place finish last season following Carrick's arrival either doesn't understand the game or is the sort of person who reads the scores but doesn't watch the matches. Action is required, because United are level on points with the third-bottom club, and if they drift further into their spiral of negativity, they risk missing out on the UEFA Champions League knockouts and the money that brings.

It's a shame, to some degree, because they looked willing and hungry in the first half Saturday, albeit against a side almost as star-crossed as they are, who gifted them numerous opportunities to score. Then Lisandro Martinez's multiple brain fades opened the door for Chelsea, and they never looked back. United fans know what's up. Their ire is rightly directed at the players, at Jim Ratcliffe (funny how that guy has gone silent), at the Glazers (the perpetual scapegoats) and Jason Wilcox (the incognito brain who assembled this team).

As for Chelsea, the three points matter, almost as much as Xabi Alonso's willingness to go 4-2-3-1 in order to find a spot for Estêvão. It's pretty grotesque that having invested so heavily on wingers the club would have signed someone who prefers the 3-4-2-1 setup. As long as you have an attacking fullback behind him (and Chelsea have three to pick from down the left) you can put Morgan Rogers out wide left and he'll be devastating. But Estêvão (or Pedro Neto, when he needs a breather) needs to play on the right. What Alonso needs most right now is a bit of stability in terms of personnel and formation. We don't need to see the back three again this season, frankly.

Bayern Munich their own worst enemy in Klassiker draw

Tell me if you've heard this before: "The biggest threat standing in the way of another Bundesliga crown for Bayern are Bayern themselves." You have, because that's the reality, such is their dominance in German football. And it holds even truer after their 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund on Saturday.

This was a game they should have put to bed. Michael Olise hit the crossbar. Harry Kane -- who paraded his well-deserved Ballon d'Or before kickoff -- hit the woodwork twice (once from a penalty). They put together 4.48 xG but scored only twice, squandering four Opta "big chances" along the way.

Regular readers will know that I don't worry about scores as much as I do performance, and the performance was there from Bayern. But this is a little different. They're still top alongside Dortmund, but obviously, the return leg will be on the road. And they lost another two players to injury in the first half -- Ismael Saibari and Serge Gnabry -- within a few minutes of each other. Early indications are they'll miss a chunk of time while Olise, thankfully, looks to have picked up a less serious knock. With Luis Díaz and Jamal Musiala in and out all season, they could be a little light up front.

This was a chance to put the first nail in the Bundesliga title race's coffin, and they flubbed it. And they were frankly a little fortunate too, because if Carney Chukwuemeka had somehow gotten out of the way of Jonas Urbig, Jobe Bellingham's goal might have stood.

As for Dortmund, we can praise their never-say-die attitude, while also recognizing that, top-to-bottom, they are several rungs below Bayern, no matter what the table says. The most you can ask for is that they keep breathing down Bayern's necks, ready to take advantage of any stumbles. Manager Nico Kovac will take that.

Quick hits

10. Seven wins on the bounce for Atlético Madrid ... and there's more to come: We recently did a segment on the FC TV show about whether Atleti could compete for the LaLiga title. The consensus seemed to be no; I was in the minority with an emphatic yes. Not just because of the semantics (what does "competitive" mean?), but because this team can legitimately get better. And while few seem to have noticed, they could actually go top next weekend if they beat Barcelona at home.

Their 2-0 win at Levante makes it seven straight. They're obviously not better than Barcelona right now, and Hansi Flick's side have a higher ceiling, but Atleti have many of the pieces in place, including Álex Baena, a guy who can create out of nothing at any time. His assist on Morten Hjulmand's disallowed goal was next level; his assist for the second wasn't bad, either. And then there's Julián Álvarez, assuming he can put his (self-inflicted) summer travails behind him. Again, I'm in the minority in not seeing why wise football folk salivate over him so much, but if they're right and I'm wrong, he can carry a team.

9. Brighton & Hove Albion go third after winning at Manchester City; can they stay there? Let me address this straight away: I think so. Or at least in the Champions League places. It's a three-point margin over Chelsea and a four-point gap over Liverpool, but even if both surpass them -- and it's not a given that they will -- Brighton will still be fifth, which will be enough if the Premier League gets the performance-based slot. We're not even a fourth of the way through the season, sure, but the other regular contenders are way back: Tottenham Hotspur (minus seven), Aston Villa (minus seven), Newcastle United (minus eight), Manchester United (minus 12).

The "Brighton model" has been much studied and copied (badly). Their scouts and recruitment guys have been poached, along with their players and coaches. And still they rise, which should tell you the secret sauce is elsewhere. Maybe it's stability: other than Jan Paul van Hecke (seamlessly replaced by Luka Vuskovic, who might actually be an upgrade) and Danny Welbeck, most of last year's big contributors are still there. They lead the league in xG but are vastly overperforming in xG conceded (they've gone up just seven, but the xG conceded is 13) so maybe they'll regress to the mean. But for now, once again, what they're doing is pretty darn special.

8. Barcelona bounce back without missing a beat: Nobody really believed that Alavés -- winless in nearly two months -- would offer much of a challenge to a Barcelona side looking to rebound after getting their nose bloodied by Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League and Real Madrid in the Clasico. But this wasn't just a victory -- it was an emphatic, slam-the-door-shut-type stomping. Being 4-0 up at halftime (en route to a 6-1 win) with 3.26 xG tells its own story.

Barcelona remain on track to break all sorts of goal-scoring records: their team goal pace is 158 and the record presently belongs to Real Madrid in 2011-12, who scored 121 under Jose Mourinho. And at this rate, Raphinha (who bagged two) will end up with 52 goals and beat Lionel Messi's single-season mark of 50. Shoutout to Flick as well. Frenkie de Jong (now fully fit) at center back gives you much-needed depth. And 20-year-old Brian Fariñas -- who made his debut at right back -- continues the tradition of playing home-grown central midfielders at fullback (witness Xavi Espart). Then again, on a team that holds 77% possession, you're basically asking your fullback to do a midfielder's job anyway.

7. Yup, Spurs have turned the corner (and not because of their win over 10-man Crystal Palace): Yes, obviously it helps tremendously when you can play 77 minutes plus stoppage time at home against 10 men, thanks to Jean-Philippe Mateta's red card (unlucky, but justified). But how often do we see teams go down a man, enter lockdown mode and successfully frustrate the opposition?

Don't let the 2-0 score fool you, though: Tottenham did not allow that to happen. They kept their shape and their principles, moved the ball to create openings and ended up with a whopping 34 shots on goal (and four "big chances" missed, none bigger than Mohammed Kudus' one at the end). As I've said before, they're much better with Dominic Solanke up front, and if that means moving Omar Marmoush into the hole (like he did Saturday) or even out wide, so be it.

Heading into the last international break, they had two points from five games. Since then, it's 10 points from four games, including away trips to Old Trafford and Stamford Bridge. I don't know that you can get away with a Sandro Tonali-Mateus Fernandes midfield most weeks in the Premier League, but manager Roberto De Zerbi has the tools to change it in terms of personnel. What matters is the patterns of play and the cohesion, and it appears Spurs have that down pat.

6. Real Madrid wrap it up early at Racing Santander, just like Mourinho likes it: Or, for that matter, any manager. Away from home this season, it has been all about the late goals: Carlos Espi at Espanyol and at Elche, Endrick and Antonio Rudiger at Roma, Kylian Mbappe in El Clasico. If games ended in the 84th minute, Real Madrid would be fifth in LaLiga, 10 points back. That's what made their 3-0 win in Santander -- who may be newly promoted, but had yet to lose at El Sardinero -- so encouraging. The big guns (Mbappe, Jude Bellingham and Yan Diomande) all scored in the first half, and they were never in danger.

Real killed the game and were able to conserve energy for the Champions League. A coach couldn't ask for more. If you want to quibble and nitpick, maybe he could have used all five substitutions and gotten some minutes for some of his bench players, but really, this was about proof of concept: After delivering in the Clasico, could they do it against a very different opponent in very different circumstances? The answer was a resounding yes.

5. Nicolas Jackson is proving doubters wrong, but Villa pay the price for Zion Suzuki's howler: I know: If my aunt had wheels, she'd be a bicycle. But bear with me. If the season began on Sept. 7, and if Suzuki hadn't let the ball slip out of his hands for the Fulham goal, or if John McGinn had converted his penalty, Villa would be third in the table, a single point behind Arsenal and Brighton. Oh, and they've also been perfect in the Champions League. All this after a summer of upheaval in which they lost Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Emiliano Martínez, Ollie Watkins, Lucas Digne and Youri Tielemans. I've said it before, but you can't repeat it enough times: If they graded on a curve, Unai Emery would be favorite for manager of the year.

That said, I want to single out Jackson, who opened the scoring Saturday. When he arrived at Chelsea, many (including me) pointed out that he was raw. And still, the club persevered with him. Then, just as he was getting good, they loaned him out to Bayern (where he scored 11 goals in limited action) and then shipped him off to Villa in the summer to assuage the Gods of Player Trading. Guess what? At 25, he's no longer raw. He has lost none of his athleticism, he's making much better decisions, and he already has eight goals in all competitions. Chelsea's backup strikers are Emmanuel Emegha and 35-year-old Welbeck. Enough said.

4. AS Roma are still on a tear: Maybe it took him a season to figure things out, but manager Gian Piero Gasperini has lost absolutely none of his relentlessness. On Saturday his Roma side stomped all over Udinese, going 4-0 up by halftime en route to a 5-2 road win that sees them move up to third in Serie A.

His Atalanta sides were legendary for their daring and attacking impetus, and Gasperini is doing the same at Roma while also putting his faith in younger players and turning older ones around. And once again, he's doing it without his starting keeper, captain, midfield general and most talented player. Roma have 36 goals in all competitions. Only Bayern (37) and Barcelona (57) -- two clubs with Ballons d'Or current and future -- have scored more. And regular Serie A watchers know the attacking fearlessness is proving infectious, with the likes of Como, Frosinone and Monza in his wake. Long may it continue. This is fun.

3. Harry who? Niclas Füllkrug is the Bundesliga's top goal scorer: It's probably just me, but I love these types of stories, so I want to get ahead of it before he invariably slips down the scoring table. For the past two seasons -- at West Ham United and at Milan -- Füllkrug has been something of a punchline. Four goals in 46 games for a center forward who doesn't do much other than score isn't great. He probably didn't take it too badly, because he was the classic late bloomer (he was in the second division just five years ago) and many turned up their nose when he was first called up to the Germany national side (and not just because of his gap-toothed smile).

But here he is, at Werder Bremen, where it all began, on loan from West Ham, and after opening the scoring in their 2-0 win over TSG Hoffenheim on Saturday, he has nine goals in eight Bundesliga appearances, plus another three in the German Cup (including two against Dortmund, no less). Füllkrug was never under any illusions when he was younger and certainly won't be now that he's 33, but it's a feel-good story that he, of all people, can tell his friends and family that the only players who have scored more this season in all competitions are Raphinha, Kylian Mbappé and Erling Haaland.

2. Alajbegovic to the rescue for Juventus against Napoli, but is it fool's gold? Another game, another system -- this time a 4-4-2 formation, though manager Luciano Spalletti says it was an emergency solution -- except this time, Juve got the three points. If you're determined to be glass half-empty, you can point out the negatives. Like the fact that the goals came late and via gorgeous (but improbable) strikes from Kerim Alajbegovic and Jeremie Boga, rather than via patterns of play. Or the fact that Napoli, who aren't particularly good to begin with and have a long injury list, lost the flu-stricken Rasmus Hojlund before kickoff and had to withdraw Kevin De Bruyne and Giovanni Di Lorenzo at halftime.

On the flip side, Alajbegovic is a legitimately gifted, fearless youngster who will only grow in confidence, and the three points should alleviate pressure on Spalletti, at least temporarily. That said, the issues are still there -- Randal Kolo Muani and Nick Woltemade had another nightmare, with just one off-target shot between them -- and won't be resolved anytime soon.

1. Home defeat highlights Manchester City's defensive issues (again): It's not that the defending was horrid, per se, on the Brighton goal (though it was) in Saturday's 1-0 defeat, or that City didn't create enough chances at the other end to get a resounding win (they did, and Bart Verbruggen made some huge saves). It's that, relative to last year, City look more fragile at the back, and that's a pretty low bar. It's not the numbers, though they're worse than a year ago in terms of xG conceded (1.30 to 1.18). It's the way they look vulnerable, especially in transition: Brighton could have added a couple of more on the break.

Enzo Maresca says he was pleased with the performance, and from his perspective, you can see why: They nearly doubled Brighton's xG, they hit the post with Iliman Ndiaye, they created at least five clear-cut chances. But as good as the attacking output is, they're not going to get where they want to be if they concede so much in transition. Ayyoub Bouaddi, making his second league start of the season, has margins to improve in that role, and the defense (all holdovers from last year) need to find the right balance to address the attacking tweaks Maresca has provided.

stories.headline: Trial begins for Guardians' Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz in pitch-rigging case
stories.summary: The trial of two major league baseball pitchers accused of rigging pitches in a betting scheme begins Monday in federal court in Brooklyn.
stories.body:
The trial of two major league baseball pitchers accused of rigging pitches in a betting scheme begins Monday with jury selection in federal court in New York.

Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase de la Cruz and Luis Leandro Ortiz Ribera are charged with conspiracy to commit wire and honest services fraud, sports bribery and money laundering.

Co-defendants Robinson Vásquez Germosen and Luis Arismendy Paca Méndez are accused of sharing inside information from Clase, 28, with other bettors and using that information to wager on what federal prosecutors say were predetermined pitches.

Paca Méndez, who prosecutors allege lived with Clase at his house in Ohio during part of the scheme, will not take part in the trial in Brooklyn after being extradited from the Dominican Republic to the U.S. on Oct. 19, according to a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York.

Guardians front office personnel, including general manager Mike Chernoff, as well as coaches and catchers who worked with Clase and Ortiz are among the potential witnesses, along with officials from Major League Baseball and DraftKings.

The government alleges that Clase, one of the best closers in baseball, rigged at least 18 pitches in 17 games from May 19, 2023, to May 28, 2025, often by intentionally throwing balls or by tipping off bettors that he would throw an off-speed pitch. Prosecutors say he shared information about the planned result or the velocity of the pitches with bettors, including Vásquez and Méndez, using code words like "rooster" and "chicken," sometimes in exchange for "bribe and kickback payments."

The bettors allegedly placed more than 100 wagers and won at least $400,000 on Clase's pitches. In a hearing Friday, attorneys disclosed that the bets were placed with DraftKings, FanDuel and ESPN BET.

Clase's attorneys have argued that his pitches were part of normal baseball strategy. "At trial, the jury will be tasked with deciding if certain ... pitches were thrown for legitimate, baseball-strategy reasons or in furtherance of a scheme to defraud betting companies," his attorneys wrote in a September filing. "In isolation, any single pitch in the dirt can be painted as nefarious."

In a January filing, Clase's attorneys said that he did not participate in a conspiracy and instead had communicated with his associates about gambling on rooster fighting in the Dominican Republic, where it is legal. They added that Clase and Ortiz moved money to their home country to buy and care for livestock, including a horse.

During the hearing Friday, prosecutors said they recently learned that Clase owes the IRS about $500,000, which they argued showed motive for the alleged bribes. Clase's attorneys denied in court that their client had a financial motive. The judge ruled the information inadmissible for trial.

ESPN obtained records of a federal tax lien listed under Clase's name in Maricopa County, Arizona, for $588,919.60 in back taxes from 2022 to 2024. The lien was issued in May 2026.

Ortiz, 27, is accused of manipulating two pitches in two Guardians games in June 2025, according to the indictment. Prosecutors say Ortiz was in debt to a company that advances money to professional athletes against their future earnings.

In a September filing, Ortiz's attorneys said that he never communicated with the bettors: "Not once. Not by text, not by phone, not in person."

"The government's case against Luis Leandro Ortiz Ribera is remarkably thin," Ortiz's attorneys wrote. "It consists, in essence, of the anticipated testimony of two cooperating bettors ... and a handful of wagers that [they] and two of their relatives placed on two pitches Mr. Ortiz threw."

The alleged scheme came to light after sportsbooks flagged unusual betting interest on Ortiz's first pitch in the bottom of the second inning on June 15, 2025, against the Seattle Mariners, and his first pitch in the top of the third inning against the St. Louis Cardinals on June 27, 2025.

In a court filing, the government said the size of the bets on the two Ortiz pitches was up to "136 times greater" than the average wager placed by the bettors allegedly involved. MLB has since asked sportsbooks to place a maximum $200 betting limit on wagers on individual pitches and to prohibit such bets from being included in parlays.

MLB placed Ortiz and Clase on non-disciplinary paid leave in July 2025. The two were indicted four months later.

Clase earned more than $13 million over a seven-year major league career, and he was scheduled to make $6.4 million in 2026. Ortiz's salary in 2025 was $782,600.

Attorneys for Clase, Ortiz and Paca Méndez did not respond to requests for comment from ESPN. A U.S. Attorney's Office spokesperson declined ESPN's request for comment about the trial.

Vásquez's attorney, Todd Spodek, told ESPN that his client is innocent.

"People forget that an indictment is just the government's side of the story," he said. "Mr. Vásquez is innocent, and we're confident that the evidence will support this."

In court documents filed days before the trial, the prosecution and defense sparred over the translation from Spanish to English of text messages, videos and voice memos that will be used as evidence. A Spanish-language interpreter will participate in the proceedings.

Judge Kiyo A. Matsumoto will oversee the trial, which the government estimates will last three weeks.

The wire fraud, honest services and money laundering charges carry maximum prison sentences of 20 years, while the sports bribery charge has a five-year maximum prison sentence, according to the Department of Justice.

The case is one of five federal sports gambling cases involving alleged performance manipulation by professional or college athletes over the past three years -- and the first to go to trial.

ESPN reporter Michael Rothstein and ESPN researcher John Mastroberardino contributed to this story.

stories.headline: Lewis Hamilton demands 'serious talks' at Ferrari, questions Charles Leclerc's 'mentality'
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton demanded "serious talks" with Ferrari as the furious British driver questioned the mentality of teammate Charles Leclerc.
stories.body:
Lewis Hamilton demanded "serious talks" with Ferrari as the furious British driver questioned the mentality of teammate Charles Leclerc.

Hamilton's first pole position in 1,197 days was undone on the opening lap as Leclerc charged through, running across the grass at Turn 4 while his wobbling teammate lost out to Max Verstappen.

That opened the door for Verstappen to take the win, while Hamilton exacted some revenge on Leclerc by passing him to claim second following a red-flag restart.

The seven-time world champion believed Ferrari had the pace to win, while they ended up separated by third-placed Kimi Antonelli as the Italian clinched the world championship.

Hamilton urged Ferrari to introduce "rules of engagement" following a coming together with Leclerc at September's Italian Grand Prix.

And he was again asking questions of his team following their latest showdown in Mexico City.

"We have to have some serious talks behind the scenes for sure," Hamilton said.

"I think the core thing to remember, which maybe comes with age, is that every decision you make in the car impacts all the people that work in the background for the whole team.

"Working as a team is a part of our job and a part of our contract. We could have easily done that today.

"This will just continue unless action is taken, unless a real deep, serious conversation is had. So, it shouldn't happen moving forward.

"Of course, the frustrations ... Today I'm happy because this guy [Antonelli] just won the championship and on the other side, I'm really p----d."

Verstappen's win saw him leapfrog Hamilton and George Russell to second in the championship, with Leclerc also in that fight. Ferrari sit second in the constructors' standings.

- How Kimi Antonelli overcame George Russell, Ferrari to become F1's youngest champion

- Kimi Antonelli's historic F1 title: Every record broken and milestone reached

Hamilton was furious on the radio during the race, accusing Leclerc of pushing him off before complaining that his teammate had only been given a five-second penalty.

He was in no mood to let up after the race.

"When your teammate works against you and then you lose positions like that, it's definitely tough," he continued.

"We don't have rules of engagement, and whether or not that will change anything from Charles' side, I don't know. Something needs to change for sure.

"Before I joined this team, when I was at Mercedes, I watched the back and forth between Charles and Carlos [Sainz], where they were battling so much that the person ahead just pulled away.

"But it is one thing when that's happening in fourth and fifth, as opposed to first and second, and you lose the win. That's significant.

"The guy [Leclerc] is 28 years old, so I don't think it's an age thing. I think it's a mentality thing.

"It's like, 'Do or die. Either I win or none of us do,' and it shouldn't be that.

"It should be us getting that one-two. You know, Silverstone, I could have gone all kamikaze on him and taken him off and lost us the win."

Leclerc suggested he would have liked to give the position back, as Hamilton asked for, but could not with Verstappen in between. He also felt the move was "on the limit" from the pair.

Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur could not hide his frustration.

"I think it's just a matter of respect," he told Sky Sports.

"The respect for the brand, for the sponsors, for the team, for the 2,000 people working at home like hell. Honestly, it's difficult to digest for me to give up a win like this.

"The comments of Lewis I will discuss with Lewis and the comments of Charles I will discuss with Charles."

stories.headline: How NBA title, MVP race has become wide open in two weeks
stories.summary: The NBA season is still young, but injuries and surprising developments have already changed narratives.
stories.body:
The 2026-27 NBA season was projected to be abnormally competitive, as previously rebuilding teams turned the corner and new draft lottery rules gave all 30 franchises an incentive to win.

At the top of the standings, though, three juggernaut rosters towered above the rest: the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs, who both won more than 60 games before clashing in a seven-game conference finals last season, and the defending champion New York Knicks, who reeled off arguably the most dominant stretch in NBA history en route to the title.

Those three teams were excellent last season, and they returned 14 of their combined 15 starters this fall. So even as the rest of the league's floor rose, the highest ceilings still appeared to reside in New York City and the Southwest.

But surprising developments have changed that narrative less than two weeks into the new season and challenged the triumvirate's hegemony atop the league. Most importantly, a wave of injuries to star players already has altered the league's most important races.

Jump to a section:

How title odds have shifted

The injured stars so far

Is the MVP race wide open?

Scuffling preseason favorites
Oklahoma City opened its season with a firm statement of intent, with 12-point wins over the Spurs and Nuggets -- possibly the Thunder's closest competition in the West.

Then disaster struck. Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace both suffered potentially season-ending injuries in the same game, and Alex Caruso sprained his right ankle the following night. At the same time, Chet Holmgren suffered a patellar tendon tear in his right knee, which will sideline him for at least two months

So Oklahoma City has played its past couple games without four of its top six players, to predictable results: a 24-point loss in Dallas followed by a 21-point loss in Houston. The Thunder were outscored in all eight quarters across those two defeats.

The team will theoretically improve from their current doldrums once Caruso and Holmgren return, but the Thunder are in deep trouble on the perimeter without Williams and Wallace. They look far away from meaningful contention given their horrid spate of injuries.

But Oklahoma City isn't the only preseason favorite with more concerns now than two weeks ago. The Knicks are 2-4 and needed two big comebacks against Detroit and Chicago just to pick up their two wins. And the Spurs started a comparatively better 4-2, but they've looked out of sorts against the toughest competition they've faced and needed overtime to beat the injury-wracked Jazz.

It's very early, and those teams still have plenty of time to round into their best shape. But the title race already looks more open.

According to preseason projections by ESPN's Basketball Power Index (BPI), the Thunder and Spurs combined for a 50% championship probability. Add in the Knicks at 8%, and BPI gave those three favorites a roughly three-fifths chance to win the title. Yet their combined odds have since fallen to just 38%, and that's with the assumption that Wallace and Holmgren return before the playoffs.

Meanwhile, a series of second-tier contenders have started strong, which should increase their confidence that they can close the gap to the Thunder, Spurs and Knicks. The Rockets lead the way with a 5-1 record including wins over Oklahoma City and San Antonio. And in the Eastern Conference, the 76ers, Pistons and Celtics started a combined 16-3 -- meaning those three teams have fewer combined losses than the Knicks have by themselves.

That trend also serves as an argument for teams with strong rosters and ample draft assets, such as Houston and Detroit, to seriously consider making in-season trades with an eye on the Finals.

If the Thunder, Spurs and Knicks were all fully healthy and running roughshod over everyone in their paths, there might be some merit to the idea of keeping one's powder dry rather than making futile trades to try to catch the leading contenders. But if those teams still look more vulnerable than expected in a few months, the deadline could pack a more potent punch.

Even more injuries
Other prospective contenders have also borne the brunt of early-season injuries -- though none to the extent of Oklahoma City's nightmare.

Players who have already missed multiple games this season include Williams, Wallace, Caruso, Holmgren, Coby White, Kon Knueppel, Cameron Johnson, Jalen Duren, Alperen Sengun, Tyrese Haliburton, Ivica Zubac, Anthony Edwards, Paolo Banchero, Jalen Suggs, Kawhi Leonard and Jaren Jackson Jr.

That's more than a full roster's worth of stars (or star role players) who have suffered injuries within the first two weeks of the new season.

Discussion around the league generally points to increased pace and stress on the body as a reason for these injuries, while understanding that they're a mix of soft tissue problems and flukes -- like the collisions that sidelined Williams and Wallace.

It's also clear that there are no quick fixes. The NBA isn't slowing down, and more radical proposals that would change the sport to reduce wear and tear -- from a shorter schedule to 40-minute games -- are equally unlikely to happen any time soon. The injury issue is a figurative pain point for the league and a literal pain point for the players who keep getting hurt.

A (potentially) wide-open MVP race
Looking ahead to the remaining five months of the regular season, it's not just the title race that has opened to new challengers. The MVP race could also devolve into a free-for-all with one more injury.

The two most recent MVPs, who have finished first and second in the voting in some order three years running, have scuffled to start this season, with numbers well below their recent norms. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Nikola Jokic perennially rank among the most productive, efficient stars in the league, but both have looked surprisingly mortal in the early going.

Put another way, Jokic and Gilgeous-Alexander finished first and second in player efficiency rating in each of the past two seasons, and they ranked first and third in 2023-24. Jokic has led the league in PER six years in a row.

Now, Jokic ranks 24th and Gilgeous-Alexander is 16th among qualified players in PER two weeks into this season.

Of course, these comparisons come after a very small sample of play -- but even then, the stars' relative struggles are unusual. Jokic, for instance, just completed his worst five-game stretch (as measured by box plus-minus) at any point in the season since 2020, before he won his first MVP.

For Gilgeous-Alexander, the Thunder's injury issues could counterintuitively give him a better chance to win his third straight MVP. Two-time winners are typically penalized -- if only unconsciously -- by voter fatigue, as no player has won three in a row since Larry Bird in the mid-'80s. However, if Gilgeous-Alexander can keep the Thunder near the top of the Western Conference standings and post his typically exemplary statistics without as much help from teammates, then he'd have a narrative boost to overcome that bias.

Yet if he and Jokic don't live up to the incredibly high standards they set while winning multiple MVPs apiece, then it seems far-fetched to think that either could claim another trophy this season.

That leaves Victor Wembanyama as the clear favorite, and betting odds reflect that status. He's responded by playing at an MVP level so far.

But remember, Wembanyama reached only the bare minimum number of games to qualify for awards last season, and he missed out in 2024-25. If he falls short of 65 games again, he could leave behind a truly wide-open race, with a whole host of viable second-tier candidates suddenly receiving real MVP consideration.

Could Luka Doncic finally receive his long-awaited MVP moment? Could Cade Cunningham, Jayson Tatum or Jalen Brunson become the first Eastern Conference perimeter players to win MVP since LeBron James in Miami? Could 19-year-old Cooper Flagg make a play at an historic award? (The answer is yes if he keeps dominating like he did in his first five games.)

The result is a season that brims with tremendous possibility -- even more than already seemed to be the case when the new year tipped off in October.

With Halloween weekend in the rearview mirror, the next major event on the calendar is American Thanksgiving -- and all the important clues that will give us in the race for the Stanley Cup playoffs.

To get the week started, it's a four-pack of games Monday, with a wide array of storylines.

Read on for a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details.

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Vegas Golden Knights at Boston Bruins

7 p.m. ET (NHL Network) | VGK -112, O/U: 6.5

In Monday's marquee matchup, the defending Western Conference champs take on the current Atlantic Division leaders. Stathletes gives this matchup a 0.76% chance of occurring as the 2027 Stanley Cup Final, which ranks 40th.

This will also be a homecoming for Vegas center Jack Eichel (North Chelmsford, Massachusetts, and Boston University) and defenseman Noah Hanifin (Boston and Boston College). Eichel has nine goals and 15 assists in 22 career games against the Bruins (with Buffalo and Vegas), and Hanifin has five goals and 12 assists in 22 games (with Carolina, Calgary and Vegas).

Thanks in large part to Jeremy Swayman -- Eichel's and Hanifin's Olympic teammate -- the Bruins are allowing the fourth-fewest goals per game in the league (2.40), and they are a perfect 9-0-0 in games in which they score three or more goals.

Detroit Red Wings at Florida Panthers

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | FLA -175, O/U: 5.5

The Panthers, who are on a three-game winning streak, welcome the Red Wings to Sunrise. Although they are 8-4-2 overall, they have yet to win against an Atlantic Division opponent, going 0-2-0 thus far. Florida has two players in the top 15 in scoring: Matthew Tkachuk (tied for ninth with 20 points through 14 games) and Seth Jones (tied for 14th with 18 through 14).

One has to scroll down a bit farther to find Detroit's leading scorer, Alex DeBrincat, who is tied for 35th with 15 points in 14 games.

The Wings have a 3-1-0 record in games in which they serve fewer penalty minutes than their opponent. This will be a factor, given that the Panthers have the NHL's ninth-ranked power play, clicking along at a 24.2% rate.

Colorado Avalanche at Chicago Blackhawks

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -230, O/U: 5.5

On paper, this one doesn't appear to be the most competitive pairing. But, the Bruins were minus-225 against the Blackhawks on Saturday and narrowly escaped with an OT win.

This is the first of four matchups between these clubs this season, and they won't meet again until Feb. 28 -- when, presumably, each team will have a different makeup thanks to trade season.

The Avs are paced offensively by Nathan MacKinnon (24 points through 14 games), Martin Necas (18 through 14) and Artturi Lehkonen (17 through 14), while the Blackhawks have a tie atop their stat sheet between Connor Bedard (nine points through eight games) and Patrick Kane (nine through 14).

Calgary Flames at San Jose Sharks

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | SJ -135, O/U: 6.5

This was supposed to be the season in which the Sharks return to the playoffs -- and it still might be, but games against seemingly outmatched opponents have slipped away from them.

San Jose will want to stay out of the penalty box as much as possible; Calgary brings the NHL's No. 2 power play (33.3%) to the SAP Center, including three power-play goals apiece already for Matvei Gridin and Morgan Frost.

The Sharks are led in scoring by Macklin Celebrini (16 points through 13 games) and Will Smith (10 through 15), their dynamic duo.

stories.headline: Messi brings Miami back to stun Revs, clinch Champions Cup spot
stories.summary: Inter Miami CF beat the New England Revolution 2-1 on Sunday in Foxborough, Massachusetts, with Lionel Messi once again providing the magic touch, this time to ensure his team's spot in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.
stories.body:
Inter Miami CF beat the New England Revolution 2-1 on Sunday in Foxborough, Massachusetts, with Lionel Messi once again providing the magic touch, this time to ensure his team's spot in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.

The win also helped Miami leapfrog the Revs into second place in the Eastern Conference with one game remaining in the MLS regular season.

"It makes me very happy for the players and for the club, we are on the side of contributing things," Miami manager Cristian González said after the game. "We are at a club that is in continuous growth, I have players committed to us. We needed to win and we challenged ourselves on what kind of team we wanted to be."

The Revolution edged out Inter Miami in the first half, registering six total shots, five corner kicks and generating an expected goals of .75, but the match went to the break tied 0-0.

Dániel Gazdag then opened up the scoring in the initial minutes of the second half, connecting with Ilay Feingold inside the box before finding the back of the net.

Miami found a way to respond to Gazdag's strike with a goal from Germán Berterame -- set up by a deft backward header from Messi -- in the 69th minute. González then bolstered Inter Miami's attack after drawing level, substituting in Luis Suárez, who had started Miami's last 25 games.

"We knew we were going up against a rival that tries to seek out duels where they defend high, so the possibility of changes was to have depth, look for the spaces, and the one-on-one matchups. We struggled with ball possession, which at times was very passive," said González. "My message to the players is I need everyone. In this case, we believed we needed to make some changes.

"This doesn't mean this is the team that's going to start the playoffs. Everyone shows me they're eager to want to play."

Messi doubled the score for Inter Miami, dribbling past defenders outside the box and smashing a trademark low, left-footed shot past Revs keeper Matt Turner.

The Revolution almost found their way back for a draw, but Ian Fray's own goal was quickly ruled offside to let Miami off the hook after it looked like Messi's heroics had been undone.

Ultimately, it was Messi's goal that clinched Inter Miami a spot in the 2027 Champions Cup. Had Miami lost or tied the game against the Revs they would have had work left to do on Decision Day on Nov. 7 to get into North America's top club competition.

"I have no doubt that he's the best of all," González said of Messi. None of them can compare to him when it comes to respect for his colleagues. Leo at his age and what he does, from my point of view, deserves the MVP and also the Ballon d'Or. I hope he can achieve it."

Inter Miami now joins Nashville SC, the Revs and the Vancouver Whitecaps in the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup. The winner of the 2026 MLS Cup will also have a place in the Champions Cup.

The Herons now have 59 points from 33 games, and will finish the regular season with a home game against Charlotte FC that will have seeding implications ahead of the MLS playoffs.

stories.headline: How the Golden State Valkyries won the 2026 WNBA title in just two years
stories.summary: When Golden State joined the WNBA, the owner said the team would win a title within five years. The Valkyries did it in two.
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Almost exactly two years ago, Natalie Nakase sat across from Golden State owner Joe Lacob for her job interview to become the head coach of the WNBA's newest team, the Valkyries. It was October 2024, and Nakase had walked into the interview with notes on why she would be the best fit, her vision for how to build a team and what set her apart from her colleagues.

But the first 10 minutes of the conversation were led by Lacob: He told Nakase he likes to set incredibly high goals and shared how he plans to achieve them. Nakase sat up straighter and leaned in a few inches closer, enticed by Lacob's work ethic.

Near the end of the conversation, Lacob told Nakase the ultimate goal, the same one he had shared in the news conference announcing the creation of the team a year earlier: "We're going to win a championship in five years."

She slammed her fists on the table in front of them.

"Hell yeah, we're gonna win a championship," she said.

On Saturday, the Golden State Valkyries did just that, beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7 of the WNBA Finals to win their first title.

Lacob and Nakase were wrong about one thing, though. The Valkyries didn't win their first championship in five years. They did it in two.

"I walked out of that conversation with Joe like, 'I want to work for him,'" Nakase said. "More than that, I want to win that first championship for him."

After the interview, Nakase immediately called her mentors, asking them how she could deliver on Lacob's aspirations. Their biggest piece of advice was to build a clear culture, and do it with competitors who would sacrifice anything for the group.

Along with general manager Ohemaa Nyanin, Nakase set the identity she wanted for her team: scrappy, defensive-minded, no egos. The Valkyries built the team their way, facing external scrutiny nearly every step of the way. People gawked -- or even laughed -- at Lacob's proclamation. But Nakase stood strong in her belief, and in his.

Sitting next to the championship trophy with a beer in her hand Saturday, Nakase was asked if winning the title felt as she imagined it would.

"F--- yeah."

TOGETHER, NYANIN AND Nakase handpicked the players who make up Golden State's roster. During the 2024 expansion draft, the Valkyries acquired Veronica Burton, the gritty two-way guard, and Kayla Thornton, a reigning WNBA champion -- two cornerstones of the franchise -- as well as Cecilia Zandalasini, an Italian national. Tiffany Hayes, a former Sixth Player of the Year, signed in free agency, and Janelle Salaun, a French forward, signed on a training camp roster. The Valkyries used their No. 5 pick in 2025 on Juste Jocyte -- a 19-year-old from Lithuania who stayed overseas that year.

Again, their decisions were questioned. Without a star, and without a history of any success, external expectations for the Valkyries were low.

But in the 2025 postseason, this group made history, propelling the Valkyries to become the first expansion franchise in WNBA history to make the playoffs in its first season. The Valkyries were swept by the Minnesota Lynx in the first round, but it laid the foundation for what the team could build on, and made Golden State an attractive landing place for free agents.

For more than a year, the Valkyries knew whom they wanted to prioritize. Gabby Williams was part of Nyanin's original vision of the team, and Nakase met with Williams in 2025 in Turkey to pitch her on coming to Golden State. But the Seattle Storm cored Williams that offseason, guaranteeing Seattle exclusive negotiating rights with the French national. Williams remembers when she heard Lacob make his proclamation in 2023. "I was impressed, and I was enticed. It was like, this is a team I could want to play for one day," Williams said. "I thought I would finish my career in Seattle, but hearing that made me think a little bit. This guy is not playing around; he wants to win. That was eye-opening to me."

When Williams became a free agent, the Valkyries contacted her again, and Lacob joined Nakase and Nyanin in the recruitment.

"He said, 'This is why we are going to win. This is why it would be silly for you to go anywhere else. This is why we're going to have longevity. I want to build dynasties here,'" Williams said.

"Who doesn't want to come to something like that? We play this game to win championships. I've never won one, and at this point in my career, that is the top priority. ... I was so convinced that I would not win anywhere else."

One day after signing Williams, the Valkyries made another trajectory-shifting acquisition, landing Kiah Stokes after she spent four seasons and won three titles with Las Vegas, where she played alongside A'ja Wilson every day and under Nakase for one year. After Iliana Rupert announced that she would miss the 2026 season due to pregnancy, Stokes started every game, defending Angel Reese in the Finals.

Nyanin knew that these players could unlock a new level of her team. What has surprised the GM, though, is how quickly it has come together.

"You just never know if that's going to work out," Nyanin said.

It has. Williams, who was named Finals MVP thanks to a 30-point performance in Game 7, is having the best season of her career. She averaged a career-best 14.4 points and shot 34.2% from 3 -- and also finished second in Defensive Player of the Year voting and received WNBA All-Defensive first-team honors. She became the engine for Golden State's top-ranked defense, while also stepping up to be the shotmaker the Valkyries needed.

"The best part has been coming to work every day and enjoying it. Like, actually, that's a huge part of contending," Williams said. "When the playoffs started, our motivation was just -- we didn't want to stop playing together. We wanted to go as deep as we could because we knew this is the last time we could have a group like this. It's been really healing for me. It's made this season really special."

Down late in a win-or-go-home Game 3 in the first round against the Dallas Wings, Thornton pulled Burton, Williams and Kaila Charles into a huddle beneath their basket. They put their arms around each other and took a collective breath.

"It's just one of those things where [it was] an awareness of what we need," Burton said. "And in that moment, we needed to take an exhale and be together and just be present. ... That's pouring into each other and building each other up."

As Nyanin watched from the tunnel -- and as that sigh fueled their comeback and offered a glimpse of the composure Golden State, a team with no All-WNBA player selections, has possessed since its inception, Nyanin knew that all of the pieces she put together fit perfectly.

"That was the epitome of things we have said to them here and there," Nyanin said. "In that moment, all of the little things we have put together, I took a breath as well just to say yes, they will fight with each other and for each other. That's exactly why I am doing the job I am doing."

NAKASE WOULDN'T LET her players pick up a ball for the first three days of training camp this season.

There was no shooting, no running plays, no offense. The first three days of camp were dedicated to defense.

"That's when I knew this was going to be different," Burton said.

Those early sessions set the tone for what Nakase would demand: consistent defensive intensity, attention to detail and execution on the game plan. It also gave her players a taste of the kind of coach she is -- one who plays battle sounds during practice and calls her players "killers," doesn't allow for celebrations, and believes that cursing just means you're telling the truth.

Even when Nakase's behavior seems jarring -- or as she puts it, extreme -- she has built an environment that encourages her players to speak up and feel respected. It's why they so willingly buy into Nakase's vision and style.

"She's so authentic," Williams said. "We know her intentions are to put us in the best position to win. ... She's passionate. And sometimes we laugh at her, but we also check on her ... it's the love we have for each other."

When Williams arrived in Golden State, she told Nakase that sometimes her delivery was confusing. Others have told Nakase that they needed more time to celebrate the smaller wins. Her coaching staff urged her to take more care of herself so she can be a better leader.

All of this experience has led the Valkyries here, to their first title. Nakase's focus on defense made Golden State's unit the top ranked in the league through the regular season -- holding opponents to a league-low 75.1 points per game -- and second best in the playoffs. Stokes had 31 blocked shots this postseason, tied with Lisa Leslie for the most in WNBA history.

And her players' feedback has pushed Nakase to be a better version of herself -- and helped turn around the Finals when Golden State trailed 2-1. After the first three games of the series, she gave herself an F-minus score on her coaching because her communication was poor. So she turned to her players to see how she -- and in turn they -- could be better.

"You can give the best scheme in the world, but if your players don't want to follow it, it's not going to be successful," Stokes said. "Her willingness to listen to us and our ideas about what we think we're best at and what we can do, that's one thing that has jumped out to me; her willingness to adapt to her players."

Heading into Game 4, Nakase inserted Hayes and Kaila Charles into the starting lineup in place of Thornton and Zandalasini, respectively. Charles finished the game with a plus-14, and Hayes added 13 points -- and the change led to a massive momentum shift in the series, with the Valkyries taking the next two games.

"The best thing about our team is no one cares who starts, no one cares," Nakase said. "We can do that because we have a really selfless team, ego-less team."

"She's a great coach for a reason," Charles. "We trust our coach, so whatever she sees, we'll execute."

As Nakase walked out of her first interview with Lacob, she pledged to herself not to let his WNBA team fail. When she began to work alongside Nyanin, she promised her that they wouldn't let each other fail. As she opened up each season with her players, Nakase made sure they had every piece of support they needed.

All of this has led to history, and the Valkyries winning a title far sooner than anyone -- even Lacob -- could have ever predicted.

"Of course this is unbelievable," Lacob said Saturday night as the Valkyries celebrated. "Two years? It's insane."
